title: Integration of Metabolism: How the Body Switches Fuels

generated.pipeline: extract → Opus draft → Sonnet accuracy gate → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: Roughly how much fat and liver glycogen does an adult carry, and how much glucose does the brain burn a day?
cards.back: About 15 kg of fat, about 100 g of liver glycogen, and about 120 g of glucose a day for the brain.
cards.quote: You carry about 15 kilograms of fat and about 100 grams of glycogen in your liver, and your brain burns about 120 grams of glucose a day.

cards.front: Liver glycogen is about 100 g and the brain burns about 120 g of glucose a day. If liver glycogen alone fed the brain, about how long would it last?
cards.back: 100 g / 120 g per day ≈ 0.83 day, about 20 hours: less than a day of the brain's glucose.
cards.quote: The fat holds months of the brain's energy; the glycogen holds less than a day of its glucose.

cards.front: Carbohydrate, fat and protein are stripped to {{c1::acetyl-CoA}}, a two-carbon fragment carried on coenzyme A, and burned in the citric acid cycle.
cards.back: Some amino acids enter as other citric acid cycle intermediates instead.
cards.quote: Carbohydrate, fat and protein are stripped to acetyl-CoA, a two-carbon fragment carried on coenzyme A
cards.section: The one-way funnel: why fat cannot become glucose

cards.front: In animals, why can acetyl-CoA not be converted back to pyruvate?
cards.back: Pyruvate dehydrogenase turns pyruvate into acetyl-CoA and releases CO₂, and in animals the step cannot run in reverse.
cards.quote: Pyruvate dehydrogenase turns pyruvate into acetyl-CoA and releases CO₂.
cards.section: The one-way funnel: why fat cannot become glucose

cards.front: Track carbons through one turn of the citric acid cycle: acetyl-CoA joins oxaloacetate, and the cycle runs back to oxaloacetate. How many extra oxaloacetate carbons are left for glucose?
cards.back: Acetyl-CoA (2) + oxaloacetate (4) = citrate (6). Two CO₂ are released (6 → 5 → 4) before oxaloacetate returns. 2 in, 2 out: net gain 0.
cards.quote: Two carbons in, two out: no extra oxaloacetate for glucose.
cards.section: The one-way funnel: why fat cannot become glucose

cards.front: Which parts of stored fat can become glucose in humans?
cards.back: Only the glycerol backbone (about a tenth of fat's mass) and a little from odd-chain fatty acids. Ordinary fatty acids cannot.
cards.quote: Of fat, only the glycerol backbone, about a tenth of its mass, and a little from odd-chain fatty acids can become glucose.
cards.section: The one-way funnel: why fat cannot become glucose

cards.front: Why do red blood cells depend absolutely on glucose?
cards.back: They have no mitochondria, so glycolysis is their only source of ATP.
cards.quote: Red blood cells have no mitochondria, so glycolysis is their only source of ATP.
cards.section: The one-way funnel: why fat cannot become glucose

cards.front: Long-chain fatty acids do reach brain tissue. Why can they not replace glucose as the brain's main fuel?
cards.back: Astrocytes burn some, but fatty acids supply only a minor share of the brain's energy; neurons rely on other fuels (glucose, and ketone bodies in a fast).
cards.quote: Long-chain fatty acids reach brain tissue, and astrocytes burn some, but they supply only a minor share of the brain's energy; neurons rely on other fuels.
cards.section: The one-way funnel: why fat cannot become glucose

cards.front: Fasting is glucose rationing. Name the three moves a healthy fasting adult makes.
cards.back: (1) Low insulin switches every tissue that can burn fat over to fat. (2) The liver supplies glucose, first from glycogen, then by gluconeogenesis from glycerol and amino acids. (3) The liver makes ketone bodies so the brain needs less glucose.
cards.quote: So fasting is glucose rationing: Low insulin switches every tissue that can burn fat over to fat.
cards.section: The one-way funnel: why fat cannot become glucose

cards.front: Insulin rises after a meal and means {{c1::store}}; glucagon rises when blood glucose falls and means release.
cards.quote: Insulin rises after a meal and means store.
cards.section: One signal, read differently by each tissue

cards.front: Why does the liver respond to the insulin-to-glucagon ratio rather than to either hormone alone, and why does it see them first?
cards.back: Both hormones push its enzymes in opposite directions, so the liver reads their balance. Both enter the portal vein, which runs straight to the liver, so it meets them first and at the highest concentrations.
cards.quote: Because they push its enzymes in opposite directions, the liver responds to their balance, the insulin-to-glucagon ratio.
cards.section: One signal, read differently by each tissue

cards.front: In fed muscle, insulin brings {{c1::GLUT4}} to the cell surface, so muscle takes up glucose and stores glycogen.
cards.quote: takes up glucose (insulin brings GLUT4 to the surface), stores glycogen
cards.section: One signal, read differently by each tissue

cards.front: Muscle holds three to four times as much glycogen as the liver. Predict whether it helps hold up blood glucose overnight, and explain.
cards.back: No. Glycogen breaks down to glucose-6-phosphate, which is trapped in the cell; only cells with glucose-6-phosphatase (chiefly liver and kidney) can free the glucose.
cards.why: Muscle also lacks glucagon receptors, so it keeps its glycogen for its own work when epinephrine or hard exercise calls.
cards.quote: only cells with glucose-6-phosphatase (chiefly liver and kidney) can remove it.
cards.section: One signal, read differently by each tissue

cards.front: How does glucagon stop glycogen synthesis and start glycogen breakdown in the liver at the same moment?
cards.back: Glucagon raises cyclic AMP, which turns on PKA. PKA's phosphates switch glycogen synthase off and glycogen phosphorylase (through phosphorylase kinase) on.
cards.quote: In the liver, glucagon raises cyclic AMP, which turns on protein kinase A (PKA).
cards.section: One signal, read differently by each tissue

cards.front: Liver cells are engineered so that PKA cannot be activated. Glucagon arrives. Predict what happens to glycogen synthase, glycogen phosphorylase and glycogen breakdown.
cards.back: Glucagon's cAMP/PKA phosphorylation of synthase and phosphorylase would not occur, so the switch from storing to breakdown fails.
cards.why: Glucagon's switch runs through cAMP and PKA phosphorylation of both enzymes.
cards.quote: PKA's phosphates switch glycogen synthase off and glycogen phosphorylase (through phosphorylase kinase) on, so storing stops and breakdown starts at once.
cards.section: One signal, read differently by each tissue

cards.front: Glucagon signaling keeps {{c1::acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC)}}, the first enzyme of fat synthesis, phosphorylated and off.
cards.back: The key phosphate is added mainly by AMPK; insulin reverses it mainly through a phosphatase.
cards.quote: Glucagon signaling also keeps acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC), the first enzyme of fat synthesis, phosphorylated and off
cards.section: One signal, read differently by each tissue

cards.front: ACC's product, {{c1::malonyl-CoA}}, normally blocks the carnitine shuttle (CPT1) that lets fatty acids into mitochondria.
cards.quote: ACC's product, malonyl-CoA, normally blocks the carnitine shuttle (CPT1) that lets fatty acids into mitochondria.
cards.section: One signal, read differently by each tissue

cards.front: A healthy adult fasts. A fasting record shows blood glucose about 3.5–4 mM, ketones about 7–8 mM (mostly β-hydroxybutyrate). About how far into the fast is this, and where does glucose come from?
cards.back: About 5 weeks. New glucose only, about 40 g a day from the liver, with the kidney making about as much again; the brain burns about two-thirds ketones.
cards.quote: new glucose only, about 40 g a day, with the kidney now making about as much again
cards.section: One person's fast, from lunch to five weeks

cards.front: From 2 hours to 5 weeks of fasting, blood glucose falls only from about 6–7 mM to about 3.5–4 mM, while ketones rise from about 0.1 mM to about 7–8 mM. What does this pattern show?
cards.back: Blood glucose is defended within a narrow band while the liver's source of it changes completely (storing, then glycogen, then new glucose) and ketones rise to stretch the glucose ration.
cards.quote: After the first hours blood glucose drifts down only modestly while the liver's source of it changes completely.
cards.section: One person's fast, from lunch to five weeks

cards.front: During a fast, what is the major fuel for muscle and liver, and which tissue supplies it?
cards.back: Free fatty acids, released by fat tissue.
cards.quote: Fat tissue releases free fatty acids, the major fuel for muscle and liver, which the funnel keeps from becoming glucose.
cards.section: The first day: store, then spend glycogen

cards.front: What are the substrates of gluconeogenesis, and which amino acid does each organ chiefly use?
cards.back: Lactate, glycerol and amino acids: chiefly alanine for the liver, glutamine for the kidney.
cards.quote: makes glucose from lactate, glycerol and amino acids (chiefly alanine for the liver, glutamine for the kidney)
cards.section: Where the new glucose comes from

cards.front: Why does the Cori cycle give the brain no new glucose?
cards.back: It sends the same carbon around again (glucose to lactate to glucose). The brain burns nearly all of its glucose to CO₂, which does not come back; only glycerol and amino-acid carbon skeletons add new carbon.
cards.quote: The brain is the drain; only glycerol and the carbon skeletons of amino acids from broken-down protein bring new carbon.
cards.section: Where the new glucose comes from

cards.front: The liver spends about 6 ATP equivalents (4 ATP + 2 GTP) to rebuild one glucose from lactate, and glycolysis gains 2 ATP. What is the net energy cost of one turn of the Cori cycle?
cards.back: 6 − 2 = a net cost of about 4 ATP equivalents per glucose cycled.
cards.quote: at a cost to the liver of about 6 ATP equivalents (4 ATP and 2 GTP) per glucose rebuilt, against 2 ATP gained by glycolysis
cards.section: Where the new glucose comes from

cards.front: In the glucose-alanine cycle, what does muscle send the liver, and what does the liver do with each part?
cards.back: Carbon and nitrogen as alanine. The carbon is a gluconeogenic substrate (partly recycled glucose); the nitrogen is dumped as urea.
cards.quote: muscle exports carbon and nitrogen as alanine, handing the liver a gluconeogenic substrate
cards.section: Where the new glucose comes from

cards.front: In a long fast, rank lactate, glycerol and muscle amino acids as sources of new glucose carbon for the brain, and state the cost of the one that supplies the most.
cards.back: Lactate adds none (Cori recycling). Glycerol adds new carbon but only about 15–20 g a day. Amino acids from muscle protein are the main new source, at the cost of muscle, with nitrogen disposed of as urea.
cards.why: Rests on the brain being a carbon drain and only glycerol and amino-acid skeletons bringing new carbon.
cards.quote: The film lists them as equals: as chemistry they are, as accounting they are not.
cards.section: Where the new glucose comes from

cards.front: Why does a fasting liver burning fat flat out make acetyl-CoA faster than its citric acid cycle can use it?
cards.back: The liver needs only so much ATP, and its oxaloacetate, which acetyl-CoA needs to enter the cycle, is being pulled toward gluconeogenesis. The surplus becomes ketone bodies.
cards.quote: its oxaloacetate, which acetyl-CoA needs to enter the cycle, is being pulled toward gluconeogenesis
cards.section: By day three: ketogenesis in full swing

cards.front: By day three of a fast, hepatic ACC is phosphorylated and off. Predict fatty acid entry into liver mitochondria, and explain.
cards.back: Entry rises sharply. With ACC off, malonyl-CoA is low, so the carnitine shuttle (CPT1) opens and fatty acids pour into the mitochondria for β-oxidation.
cards.quote: Malonyl-CoA is low, so the carnitine shuttle opens and fatty acids pour into the liver's mitochondria.
cards.section: By day three: ketogenesis in full swing

cards.front: Which enzyme does the liver lack, so that it cannot burn the ketone bodies it makes?
cards.back: SCOT, which reactivates acetoacetate into acetoacetyl-CoA. The liver ships its ketone bodies to brain, heart and muscle.
cards.quote: Lacking SCOT, the enzyme that reactivates acetoacetate into acetoacetyl-CoA for burning, the liver ships everything it makes to the brain, heart and muscle.
cards.section: By day three: ketogenesis in full swing

cards.front: Besides the malonyl-CoA gate on CPT1, which liver enzyme does fasting raise to commit acetyl-CoA to ketone bodies?
cards.back: Mitochondrial HMG-CoA synthase.
cards.quote: fasting raises mitochondrial HMG-CoA synthase, the liver enzyme that commits acetyl-CoA to ketone bodies
cards.section: Glycogen and ketogenesis, in detail

cards.front: A drug keeps hepatic ACC active during a fast, so malonyl-CoA stays high. Predict ketone body production and the effect on the brain's glucose demand.
cards.back: Ketogenesis falls: malonyl-CoA keeps CPT1 blocked, so fatty acids cannot enter the mitochondria for β-oxidation. With fewer ketones, the brain must keep burning more glucose.
cards.why: Rests on the malonyl-CoA gate on CPT1 being the main driver of ketogenesis.
cards.quote: Beyond the malonyl-CoA gate on CPT1, the main driver,
cards.section: Glycogen and ketogenesis, in detail

cards.front: Suppose the brain burned only glucose (120 g a day) and glycerol supplied about 15–20 g of it. How much glucose a day must come from amino acids, and about how much muscle protein does that cost?
cards.back: 120 − (15 to 20) ≈ 100–105 g of glucose a day from amino acids, costing about 180 g of muscle protein a day.
cards.quote: Glycerol covers about 15–20 grams, so the main raw material would be your own muscle protein, about 180 grams a day.
cards.section: Weeks: the brain switches, and muscle is spared

cards.front: A 70 kg adult has roughly 10 kg of protein. At 180 g of protein a day, about how long until a third of it is gone?
cards.back: 10,000 g / 3 ≈ 3,333 g; 3,333 / 180 ≈ 18.5 days, about two and a half weeks. Rough sums: measured loss in prolonged starvation is nearer 20 g a day.
cards.quote: about 180 g of protein a day would strip a third of the body's roughly 10 kg of protein in about two and a half weeks
cards.section: The protein arithmetic

cards.front: What properties let ketone bodies replace most of the brain's glucose in a long fast?
cards.back: They are small and water-soluble, so they cross into the brain, and the brain takes up more of them as blood levels climb.
cards.quote: Ketone bodies are the escape: small and water-soluble, they cross into the brain.
cards.section: Weeks: the brain switches, and muscle is spared

cards.front: After weeks of fasting the brain's glucose need falls to roughly 40 g a day, and the protein bill for the brain's share falls to about a fifth of 180 g a day. What is the new bill, and why does it matter?
cards.back: 180 / 5 ≈ 36 g of protein a day. This protein-sparing effect is what makes a long fast survivable.
cards.quote: Its glucose need falls to roughly 40 grams a day and the protein bill for the brain's share falls to about a fifth.
cards.section: Weeks: the brain switches, and muscle is spared

cards.front: In a fasting animal, ketone uptake into the brain is blocked. Predict the brain's glucose need and the rate of muscle protein loss.
cards.back: The brain stays on glucose, about 120 g a day, so gluconeogenesis must draw heavily on muscle protein (about 180 g a day by the rough sums) instead of about a fifth of that.
cards.why: Rests on the ketone switch being what spares muscle protein.
cards.quote: If the brain burned only glucose, gluconeogenesis would have to make all 120 grams a day.
cards.section: Weeks: the brain switches, and muscle is spared

cards.front: In untreated type 1 diabetes, blood glucose sits near 25 mM, about five times the overnight level. Predict blood ketones, and explain.
cards.back: High: usually above 3 mM, and 10–20 mM or more in severe cases. With insulin absent and glucagon high, fat breakdown and ketogenesis run unopposed: diabetic ketoacidosis.
cards.quote: High: usually above 3 mM, and in severe cases 10–20 mM or more.
cards.section: When the brake is missing: diabetic ketoacidosis

cards.front: A person in diabetic ketoacidosis is given insulin. Predict the changes in fat breakdown, hepatic ketogenesis and muscle glucose uptake, and name the rule.
cards.back: Fat breakdown slows (insulin's brake returns), ketogenesis falls (ACC back on, malonyl-CoA blocks CPT1), and muscle takes up glucose again (GLUT4 to the surface).
cards.why: Tissues respond to the hormone signal, not directly to the blood glucose level.
cards.quote: Tissues respond to the hormone signal, not directly to the blood glucose level.
cards.section: When the brake is missing: diabetic ketoacidosis

cards.front: Insulin and glucagon set the bifunctional enzyme PFK-2/FBPase-2, whose product, {{c1::fructose-2,6-bisphosphate}}, chooses between glycolysis and gluconeogenesis.
cards.quote: whose product, fructose-2,6-bisphosphate, chooses between glycolysis and gluconeogenesis
cards.section: Reciprocal control

cards.front: What does AMPK sense, and what does it do when ATP runs low?
cards.back: The AMP:ATP and ADP:ATP ratios. When ATP runs low, as in hard exercise, it shuts off building (ACC among its targets) and turns on burning.
cards.quote: When ATP runs low, as in hard exercise, it shuts off building (ACC among its targets) and turns on burning
cards.section: AMPK

cards.front: A well-fed person (insulin high) sprints hard, and ATP runs low in working muscle. Predict what AMPK does to building and burning pathways (ACC among its targets), and name the rule.
cards.back: AMPK shuts off building (ACC among its targets) and turns on burning, even though the hormones say fed.
cards.why: AMPK answers the cell's own energy stress rather than the meal clock.
cards.quote: answering the cell's own energy stress rather than the meal clock
cards.section: AMPK

cards.front: How can odd-chain fatty acids give a little glucose when even-chain ones cannot?
cards.back: They end in propionyl-CoA, which becomes succinyl-CoA, a citric acid cycle intermediate that can be drawn off toward glucose.
cards.quote: Odd-chain fatty acids end in propionyl-CoA, which becomes succinyl-CoA, so they give a little glucose.
cards.section: Two small exceptions

cards.front: Plants and many bacteria have the glyoxylate cycle. Predict which step of the citric acid cycle it bypasses, and whether mammals have it.
cards.back: It bypasses the citric acid cycle's two CO₂ steps. Mammals lack it.
cards.quote: Plants and many bacteria bypass the cycle's two CO₂ steps with the glyoxylate cycle, which mammals lack.
cards.section: Two small exceptions

cards.front: A person cannot make liver glucose-6-phosphatase. After an overnight fast, predict whether liver glycogen can support blood glucose, and whether muscle glycogen can make up for it.
cards.back: Liver glycogen cannot: it breaks down to glucose-6-phosphate, which stays trapped. Muscle cannot compensate either, since it also lacks the enzyme and glucagon receptors.
cards.why: Rests on the glucose-6-phosphate trap: only cells with glucose-6-phosphatase release glucose into blood.
cards.quote: Glycogen breaks down (through glucose-1-phosphate) to glucose-6-phosphate, whose phosphate traps the sugar in the cell
cards.section: One signal, read differently by each tissue

cards.front: An adult carries months of energy as fat, yet in a long fast spends muscle protein to make glucose. Explain why, and how ketone bodies limit the cost.
cards.back: Fatty acids cannot become glucose (PDH is one-way and the cycle loses two CO₂), yet brain and red cells need glucose, so new glucose must come from glycerol and amino acids. Ketones replace most brain glucose, cutting the protein bill.
cards.why: Combines the one-way funnel with the brain's switch to ketone bodies.
cards.quote: Yet in a long fast the body guards its glucose and spends muscle to do it.
